newsitem.title: USA: Croatia's Granic rebuts U.S. criticism.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's Granic rebuts U.S. criticism.

text.p: Senior Croatian officials, smarting from strong U.S. criticism, on Friday insisted Zagreb will meet Dayton peace accord requirements concerning Serbs and war criminals but said they needed $500 million to do so.

Croatian Foreign Minister Mate Granic challenged the U.S. State Department's description of his meeting with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Thursday and said the two agreed on "more than 90 percent" of the issues they discussed.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Albright scolded Granic in a 50-minute meeting on Thursday over Croatia's treatment of Serbs and other peace accord violations.

It was the clearest public signal yet of increased U.S. frustration with Croatian President Franjo Tudjman, whose tone has turned increasingly nationalistic and whose ties with American diplomats have deteriorated.

The secretary's complaints included specific incidents of Croatian mob violence against minority Serbs in Eastern Slavonia and of Croatia's refusal to allow Serbs to return to their homes in the Krajina region of the country, Burns said.

Croatian officials have often asserted a commitment to the 1995 U.S.-mediated Dayton Peace accords which ended the war in Bosnia, but failed to follow up. Albright was not satisfied with Granic's responses, Burns said.
Granic said Burns statement "doesn't fully reflect the discussion" with Albright and insisted: "We were in agreement on more than 90 percent of these issues."
"Our strategic aim is really to return all the people from Eastern Slavonia who want to return on a voluntary basis," Granic told a news conference.
Zagreb plans to "work very hard to return these people ... protect the people and to give full guarantees for protection of minority rights and human rights," he said.
As for the Bosnia war crimes tribunal in the Hague, Granic said: "Croatia is ready to fully cooperate."

Granic said Albright provided "new information about the problems of refugees (and) cooperation with the Hague tribunal" on Bosnia war crimes and "we gave really many answers on all these issues in detail."

Washington has long demanded that Croatia send indicted war criminals to the Hague for prosecution. Albright reported that Dario Kordic, a Bosnian Croat leader charged with murdering hundreds of Moslems in 1993, was in Croatia but Granic said he did not believe that was so.

The Eastern Slavonia enclave of Croatia, a once-volatile region dominated by Serbs and bordering the Yugoslav republic of Serbia, is now administered by the United Nations under a mandate expiring on July 15. It will then become part of Croatia proper and revert to Zagreb's control.

Serbs and human rights monitors have reported that Bosnian Croat refugees expelled and abused elderly Serbians in central Croatia, threatening them with bombs and smashing windows. Key to the Dayton accords is that displaced people should be able to return home.
Granic said that in 1991-1995 when Serbs occupied one-third of Croatia, thousands of Croats were killed or expelled from their homes and that as a result, hostile feelings linger.
Integration was going "very well" and "our government is ready to take full control ... investigate all the incidents and prevent the incidents" between Serbs and Croats, he said.

But Jure Radic, development and reconstruction minister, said Croatia needs $1 billion over two years to build houses so refugees and the displaced can be resettled. Half of that would come from Croatia's budget and the rest was being sought from the world community, he said.
